clue.text: Rose to the occasion, dressed in ceremonial cloak

definitions.meaning: managed well when faced with a challenge, past tense
wearing a cope, the long cloak a priest wears at ceremonies

explanation.definitionFit: To cope is to manage a difficulty, and a cope is a priest's ceremonial cape, so a cleric wearing one is so attired.

clue.text: Giving way as a result 'of trouble with A I changeover

indicators.note: the letters A and I swap places, so the A jumps past the I in the word for trouble

parts.note: a complaint is a trouble, as in a medical complaint

explanation.surface: Someone yields after a computer system's upgrade causes difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With A I changeover' swaps the A and I in COMPLAINT. The scan prints 'A 1', with the 1 standing for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone compliant yields readily to others' wishes, obedient rather than resistant.

clue.text: Oriental dish — one, figuring in the Letters of Paul

indicators.note: appearing within, so the numeral-letter for one sits inside the rearranged name
the letters of the name are taken and reordered rather than read as written

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A rice dish turns up in the Epistles of St Paul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters of' rearranges PAUL into PLAU, and 'figuring in' puts I inside it. The Letters of Paul look like the Epistles in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilau is spiced rice cooked in stock, a dish from the Middle East and South Asia.

clue.text: How the Israelites crossed, river in shoddy resort

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, so the river letter sits within the shuffled word
to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A biblical crossing is set against a run-down holiday town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' reads as a seaside town but means re-sort: SHODDY becomes DYSHOD, and 'in' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israelites crossed the Red Sea on dry ground with feet unwetted, which is what the compound means.

clue.text: Take steps to make this recorder work

definitions.text: Take steps to make this recorder work

parts.words: Take steps to make this recorder work
parts.note: the device counts a walker's paces, so one must literally walk for it to register anything

explanation.surface: Advice on taking action to get a tape machine going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take steps' sounds like 'take action', but here it means walking.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument counts paces as its wearer walks, so it records nothing until the user moves.

clue.text: Fence losing colour

definitions.meaning: a barrier of stakes or pales

explanation.definitionFit: A fence of upright stakes is a paling, and anyone blanching from shock is going pale.

clue.text: Only half a man, but has lots 'of bottle

parts.note: demi- is a prefix meaning half
John is a man's name

explanation.surface: A coward is only half a man, yet shows great courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for courage, which the surface uses; the definition means a large bottle holding a lot of liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: This vessel is a big narrow-necked glass jar, often wicker-covered, holding several gallons of wine.

clue.text: Indian booked at the end 'of the line

definitions.text: booked at the end 'of the line
definitions.meaning: the title character of the novel 'The Last of the ...', so the last of the line in a book

explanation.definitionFit: This North American tribe is named in Fenimore Cooper's novel about the final survivor of a dying line.

clue.text: Sailor-apostle wearing waterproof hat

parts.note: a tar is an old word for a sailor
St Paul is called the apostle to the Gentiles
dressed in, so wearing gives the little word in

explanation.surface: A seafaring saint dons a rain hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' reads as the link to the hat but supplies the letters IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors once wore a hat of tarred canvas, called by the same name as the tarred sheet, to keep out rain.

clue.text: Football representatives are backs

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a code of football
MPs are Members of Parliament, elected representatives

explanation.surface: A football club's officials turn out to be its defenders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backs' looks like the defensive players but means backsides.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindquarters or bottoms are a person's or animal's rear ends.

clue.text: Language written forwards or backwards in India

indicators.text: written forwards or backwards in India
indicators.note: the language's name spells the same either way round, and it is spoken in India

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An Indian tongue whose script can go either direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The name reads the same both ways; it is the language of Kerala in south-west India.
explanation.definitionFit: This Dravidian tongue is spoken mainly in the Indian state of Kerala.

clue.text: Muslim women's collective

parts.note: the wives and concubines of a household considered together, sounding like a cooperative or union

explanation.surface: A women's cooperative in a Muslim community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collective' suggests a cooperative or workers' group; here it is the noun for the women as a body.
explanation.definitionFit: In a traditional Muslim household the wives and concubines together are known collectively by this word.

clue.text: Kookaburra having no problems with a donkey

parts.note: the idiom 'you're laughing' means you are well placed, with no worries
a jackass is a male donkey

explanation.surface: An Australian bird manages fine alongside a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laughing' as 'having no problems' is a British idiom: if you're laughing, things are going well.
explanation.definitionFit: The kookaburra, an Australian kingfisher, is nicknamed for its call that sounds like raucous mirth.

clue.text: A royal rebel — Burlington, perhaps?

parts.note: R stands for royal, as in RN, Royal Navy
Jack Cade led the Kentish rebellion of 1450

explanation.surface: A royal rebel, maybe someone named Burlington.
explanation.walkthrough: Burlington looks like a person's name; the Burlington Arcade is a covered shopping passage in London's Piccadilly.
explanation.definitionFit: London's famous covered shopping passage off Piccadilly is an example of this kind of walkway.

clue.text: Do tricks before the magistrate — imagine!

parts.note: to conjure is to perform magic tricks
up means in court, as in 'up before the beak'

explanation.surface: A magician performs in front of a judge, astonishingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' as 'appearing in court' is British: to be up before the magistrate is to face charges.
explanation.definitionFit: To call something up in the mind is to picture it, so the phrase means to bring forth from imagination.

clue.text: Surely this American writer wasn't just a corn-merchant?

definitions.text: Surely this American writer wasn't just a corn-merchant?

parts.words: Surely this American writer wasn't just a corn-merchant?
parts.note: the surname of the author of The Big Sleep is also the old trade word for a dealer, as in corn ...

explanation.surface: A doubtful question about a famous novelist's real trade.
explanation.walkthrough: A corn chandler was a grain dealer; Raymond Chandler wrote The Big Sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler was the American crime novelist, and his surname is also the trade name for a dealer in supplies.

clue.text: The awful Carker swallows his tea, talking to swindler

indicators.note: takes in, so one piece goes inside the shuffled name
badly made, so the letters of the name are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written: the villain of Dickens's Dombey and Son

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so a word that sounds like the drink is used

parts.note: the drink tea, said out loud

explanation.surface: Dickens's villain Carker gulps his tea while chatting to a conman.
explanation.walkthrough: James Carker is the villain of Dickens's Dombey and Son, so the surface reads as a scene from the novel. 'The' and 'his' are only links; tea becomes TEE because the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone running a fraudulent or extortionate scheme is a crook who cheats people.

clue.text: Fine cutter was no net return

indicators.note: come back, so the three words are read in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A precise blade turned out to be no net gain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' looks like profit, but it reverses WAS NO NET letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This small fine-toothed saw cuts the projecting tongue of a joint, a precise woodworking tool.

clue.text: Turn round a learner driver is having 'little bumps!

indicators.note: change, so the letters of round, a and the learner letter are reordered

parts.note: L is the plate for a learner driver

explanation.surface: A learner driver doing a U-turn hits a bumpy surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn round' looks like one instruction; 'Turn' alone rearranges ROUND, A and L, the L-plate letter, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something covered in small knobs or lumps is studded with nodules.

clue.text: Like a dramatic device, right in Greek

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, so the letter for right sits within the Greek word

parts.note: Ionic is a Greek order of architecture and a Greek dialect

explanation.surface: A theatrical technique works well in Greek drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatic device' is dramatic irony, where the audience knows what a character does not.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramatic irony is a stage technique, so something sarcastic or contradictory has that quality.

clue.text: Wild osier with soft and hard fruit

indicators.note: untamed, so the letters of the willow word and the two letters are mixed up

parts.note: P is piano, soft in music
H is hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A wild willow bears both soft and hard fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges OSIER plus P and H; an osier is a willow used for basketwork.
explanation.definitionFit: The red seed-pod of the wild briar is a fruit used for syrup.

clue.text: These birds don't exist. Do rabbits 'or deer?

parts.note: female rabbits and deer are both called does

explanation.surface: A question about whether extinct birds are like rabbits or deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is taken as written, and 'Do rabbits or deer?' reads like a question about extinction.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct flightless birds of Mauritius no longer survive, an older plural spelling.

clue.text: Once this is laid down, everything gets piled on top

definitions.text: Once this is laid down, everything gets piled on top

parts.words: Once this is laid down, everything gets piled on top
parts.note: reads like a mess heaped up, but describes the ceremonial first block of a building

explanation.surface: Once one thing is set down, everything else is heaped on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests clutter piling up; the building rises on the block laid first.
explanation.definitionFit: This ceremonial block is laid at the start of building work and the walls rise upon it.

clue.text: Consult this panel to check your progress

definitions.text: Consult this panel to check your progress

parts.words: Consult this panel to check your progress
parts.note: sounds like an advisory board, but is a car's instrument board showing speed and distance

explanation.surface: Advice to seek feedback from a committee on how you're doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panel' suggests a group of advisers; it is the dashboard of a car, whose instruments show speed and distance.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's dashboard holds the speedometer and mileage dial, so a driver reads it to track the journey.

clue.text: Morris dancers displaying gold lace

indicators.note: showing, so the answer is on view inside the words

explanation.surface: Morris dancers showing off their golden trimmings.
explanation.walkthrough: Morris dancing is an English folk dance with bells and ribbons.
explanation.definitionFit: This old term names lace or braid woven with gold or silver thread.

clue.text: Indian lake may have fish in it

parts.note: the Cree are a North American people

explanation.surface: An Indian lake might be stocked with fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' suggests India, but it is a Native American people.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler's wicker basket holds the day's catch.

clue.text: Old locomotive, very hard to mount

parts.note: iron is proverbially hard
a horse is a mount, something ridden

explanation.surface: An old steam engine is very hard to climb onto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To mount' reads as a verb but supplies the noun for a ridden animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Early railway engines were nicknamed after the animal they replaced, made of metal.

clue.text: Delicacy at the table — like, father returning the sugar? .

parts.note: as means like, in the same way
pa is a familiar word for father

indicators.note: going back, so the sweet word is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: At dinner, a father passes back the sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' reverses SUGAR to give RAGUS, so the dinner-table picture of handing back the sugar bowl is false.
explanation.definitionFit: The tender green spears are a prized vegetable served as a luxury course.

clue.text: There may be a catch here — yes, it's a sitter

definitions.text: There may be a catch here
definitions.meaning: a tricky question or puzzle, one with a hidden snag
a person modelling for an artist or photographer

explanation.definitionFit: A puzzling problem has a trick in it, and a model holds still for a portrait.
